utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. President. Representing General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mr. Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Representing Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber would like to greet everybody in the courtroom, representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as everybody present in the courtroom. We shall now continue with the testimony we started yesterday. We are in Courtroom II, which is much more -- cosier, because we are very close to each other. We could not work in Courtroom III, but when we have the map, which we need today, maybe we can stick it to the wall if possible. Mr. Bourgon has to take into account the size of the map and the size of the courtroom to see whether this would be possible. I don't know whether the registry has taken this into consideration when choosing the courtroom. Can Madam Usher please bring the witness into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. It seems that we have a minor technical problem with the audio system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe in that case it would be good if the registrar could call the technician into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you please put on your headphones and check whether you can hear me. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Mr. Bourgon, do you still have the same problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this side it functions, but on the other side there's -- something seems to be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that the device was not plugged in. Am I right in thinking that? Does everything work now? If that is the case, Major, today we're going to finish your testimony. You may be sure of that. The Prosecution needs another 20 minutes. The Judges are going to put some questions to you after that. And I believe that before half past 10.00 your testimony will be over and you will be able to go back to your normal duties. Mr. Withopf, you have the floor. You can continue with your additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Withopf:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Major.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, I have five distinct areas I wish to address in following up issues that were discussed in the course of the cross-examination by my learned colleagues from the Defence. Whilst cross-examined by the Hadzihasanovic Defence, you mentioned that you came across checkpoints manned by Mujahedin. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to where you came across such checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those checkpoints I mentioned yesterday were not permanent checkpoints. Normally we had checkpoints from BiH and HVO. We had different permanent manned checkpoints, but sometimes we observed that there were temporary checkpoints manned by Mujahedins. And when I say "Mujahedins," it was normally soldiers in Arabic clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, sir, do you recall as to where you came across such temporary checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember when we were taking the mountain road from the -- I can't remember the name of the road, but we could go to Zenica by two roads, and the shortest one were from the -- on the road going from Novi Travnik and Vitez to -- following the Lasva River. And there was a road going north from that road to Zenica, and normally on that road where we time to time saw that there was a checkpoint from -- manned by members of the Mujahedins. And once we found one in another area; that was in the -- as far as I remember, on one of the roads in the Guca Gora area. But I cannot recall the exact position, but it was in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously areas within the 3rd Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the fact that Mujahedin manned temporary checkpoints, was it a repeated occurrence throughout your time in the region?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it -- of course, I made these observations in the period from -- in May and June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make such observations repeatedly?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I made those observations two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whenever you came across such temporary checkpoints manned by Mujahedin, were you allowed to pass such checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally we were allowed to pass without any problems. I can recall one time where we passed a checkpoint and after we have passed the checkpoint, they opened fire against us, but only to -- it was not to harm us, to kill us; just to show a show of force, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whenever you were given the opportunity to pass such Mujahedin checkpoints, was there any discussion with the Mujahedin manning such checkpoints prior to you allowed to pass them?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember once where the men at the checkpoint, they were having a discussion with our interpreter, a young Muslim. I didn't understand during the discussion what they were saying, but later on my interpreter told me that the Mujahedins were not -- told him that he was not a good Muslim. So they want to give him -- to teach him how to be a good Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to the next issue, Major, the detention facility in Mehurici. Yesterday in answering a question by my learned friends from the Hadzihasanovic Defence, you said: "The local ABiH commander told us that the ABiH was protecting the detained civilians against the Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any indication that the more than 200 detained civilians in the sports hall of the Mehurici school were aware that they were protected against Mujahedin, and did you get the impression that they wanted to be protected against Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I think it's a story he told us; that they were only protecting them against the Mujahedins was just a story he was telling. Because I said to him, "If you are protecting them, why are the keys sitting on the opposite side of the door and not inside the hall?" Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And the people in the area, the detained persons, they were aware that the Mujahedins were operating in that area, but they were not that afraid, so they felt themselves that they need protection from BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Let's move on to the next issue. You informed the Trial Chamber yesterday that in April 1993 you visited some Croat villages in the area and you took Father Stipan with you. Why did you take Father Stipan with you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took Father Stipan with us because he knew people in the area and he was their priest, the highest-rank priest from that church. And when we were doing our fact-finding, we would like to tell the Croats about our findings. And to be sure that they understand that we were telling the truth, we were bringing Father Stipan so he could assure the Croats that what we were telling them was correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, Major, did you consider Father Stipan a reliable person? Was the information he was providing you with correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were visiting Croat villages, Father Stipan had some information of incidents that have taken place in those villages, and sometimes we were able to confirm the incidents he told us about. And normally we trusted, him, more or less because he was a man of the church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can I please ask the registrar to provide the witness with a copy of DH167.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I understand you have the bundle of documents in front of you which were tendered into evidence yesterday by the Defence. If I may draw your attention, please, Major, to the 16th of May, 1993 report which is signed by Bent Faerge and yourself. If I may draw your attention to number 6 in this report, which reads as follows: "Mr. Merdan and Mr. Skopljak agreed this morning to release all civilians who were kept in Kaonik and Zenica; furthermore, to release all members of ABiH imprisoned in Busovaca and all members of HVO imprisoned in Zenica after May 17th, 1993." Major, do you have any knowledge as to whether the Zenica Music School formed part of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I cannot remember this agreement that are mentioned in this. I cannot remember the connection why we were going to release prisoners at this specific period, so maybe it has been some agreement in a local cease-fire or something. But I cannot remember the -- this episode.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the exhibit please be removed from the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the allegations, Major, that the ABiH kept detainees in the Zenica Music School and that they were mistreated there, was this to your knowledge ever raised with 3rd Corps; for example, with Mr. Merdan, Mr. Hadzihasanovic, or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any knowledge about the music school as a detention facility at that period. Later on, when I was chairing this joint command humanitarian commission, where I had to visit the music school, that was the first time I heard that it could have been a possibility for detained persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yesterday informed the Trial Chamber that you were not given access immediately to the music school but you had to first talk to Mr. Merdan, the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps. Did you inform Mr. Merdan as to the purpose of your visit to the music school, and did you inform him about the allegations of detainees kept there and crimes or mistreatment done in the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that Mr. Merdan knew why we were going to see the music school, because the members of the joint humanitarian commission, of course, have their consultations with their headquarters. So the two headquarters knew about what we were going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am looking at the transcript on page 8. My learned friend's question, line 3 and 4. The question put to the witness by my learned friend was whether he gave any information to Mr. Merdan regarding detainees who were allegedly detained in the music school or crimes allegedly having been committed there. I do not have the wording of what the witness said yesterday. I believe that he said that he said that he did visit the music school as the president of the humanitarian commission. He never mentioned any charges, any allegations. That was not part of the framework of his visit. He paid a visit to all the detention centres in the region, and this was not part of his mission. I would like this answer to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, yesterday the witness explained that within the framework of his tasks and duties he visited the music school in Zenica. The Defence says that the question you have put now indicates that there may have been other elements in a routine visit, or in other words, that there might have been some allegations according to which crimes were allegedly committed against the detainees and that the witness spoke about that with Mr. Merdan. Can you please rephrase your question to -- so as to make it clear. Did the witness go there knowing that somebody -- something had already happened, or did he become aware of things only subsequently? There seems to be a confusion here. I give you the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, you heard the question asked by the Presiding Judge. Can you please answer it.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were visiting the music school in Zenica, it was just because we have heard that there should be detained persons there. I haven't had any informations on what there have been -- if it has been used as a detention facility earlier than my visit, but we had heard rumours that it should be a detention facility. That's why we were visiting the music school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the last issue, Major, I wish to briefly cover with you today. Asked by my learned friends from the Kubura Defence, you yesterday informed the Trial Chamber that whilst you were visiting the Zenica Music School you did not hear anybody speaking Arabic in the music school. Whilst you've been in the music school, did you have an opportunity to talk to all soldiers in the Zenica Music School, including the ones who wore clothes of the style foreign Mujahedin usually were wearing in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only persons we had -- we spoke with were the two, maybe three persons that showed us around, and that was interpreted from the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Just exceptionally, are there any questions by the Defence? The Chamber will allow you in this case to put additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do not have any additional questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. It will be the Judges who will put questions to you. Judge Swart is going to ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there'll be no questions on behalf of Mr. Kubura. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Witness, on what you said yesterday. First on the Zenica Music School. You told us a story that you were not permitted to enter the signals room. Do you remember on what floor the signals room was?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can just remember that there was one room we didn't have access to, but I cannot remember where it was situated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The second thing you said is that, if I recall this correctly, that you had information on there being a basement. And my question is: Did you have that information before you went to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. school, or did that come afterwards?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you are looking at the school, you're able to see the basement, I think. I can't remember it correctly, but I'm sure that we have been seeing the basement, because if we didn't see the basement, it would have been very suspicious to us that if we would not have been allowed to see the basement. As I said earlier, I can recall that we was not allowed to see the room they claimed to be a signal room. If they have denied us access to a basement, I'm sure that I could remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you mentioned this detail on your own initiative. You came to it wholly by yourself. So this must have some meaning to you, some importance.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the basement? No, just because yesterday I was showed a picture by the Prosecutor showing the basement, but I could not recall the picture of the basement. But I'm sure that I have -- when you are in a building, you can see there's a stair going down, and I would have been suspicious if I was not allowed to go downstairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you didn't ask for it.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the basement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because we were showed around in -- in the whole building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. So to summarise, you were aware that there was a basement, but you thought to yourself That is not a place that could be interesting for us.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I have been in this building and the only room I didn't see in the building was a room they claimed to be the signal room. And the signal room was not in the basement, and I'm sure that if we have been denied access to go downstairs, using the staircase downstairs, I would have been suspicious to see why were we not allowed to go down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But I understand this was your own choice, not to go down.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I have been in the whole building except one room, but I cannot specifically remember the basement. I cannot specifically remember the other floors. But I have been on all the floors except one room. But I cannot recall the picture of the basement. And if the Prosecutor has showed me pictures of other rooms in the music school, I would not be able to remember those rooms, because things happened 11 years ago and it's very difficult to remember all rooms in that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: When you talked about the signals room, you also told, if I am remembering this well, that you saw cables coming out of that room. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And that's why we made -- or I made this conclusion that they were telling that it was correct there was a signal room in there, because it seemed to be cables for signal equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. The second questions or the second sort of questions I have is on your visit to Mehurici. You told us yesterday about visiting the school there, the gymnasium, talking with the local commander, and being informed about the reasons of the civilians being there. You also told us about an incident before or afterwards or during your visit in which you and BritBat were threatened by Mujahedin, and they pointed their arms on you and you said this was a rather tense moment or even more. And this was a confrontation, you said, with the Mujahedin. The Defence has given us a number of texts yesterday, and it was shown to you this morning in a different context. But in these texts there is also a summary, a monitoring -- a monitor team report on your visit to Mehurici, and it's basically the same as what you told us yesterday. But there is one detail I would like to ask you something about. In talking about Mujahedin in this report, you talk about the MOS.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The MOS, that was -- when we were using "MOS," I can't remember the mean of "MOS" but it was a word used for the Mujahedins, Muslim extremists. I cannot remember why it was called MOS, but MOS is the same as Muslim extremists or Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you're not quite sure what it stands for, this --

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember -- I cannot remember what "MOS" stands for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you used the expression in your report.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And what do you think MOS is ?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we were using two expressions: We were using "MOS", that was Muslim extremists, like Mujahedins; And on the opposite side, with the HVO, we were using HOS, H-O-S, for Croatian extremists. But I cannot remember what the M-O-S stands for. As well, I cannot remember what the H-O-S stands for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Who used this expression? How did you become aware of this expression?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'd used often in our reports. UNPROFOR used the same expressions in their reports as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you didn't seem to -- you don't seem to have any information about the nature of this group or organisation or whatever.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But using the expression MOS is the same as using the expression "Mujahedins."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So it's interchangeable for you, the two expressions.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Sometimes we used "MOS" because it's much easier to type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Who spoke to you about MOS? Is that the people themselves, the Mujahedin, as you said before?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Have you heard people using the word "MOS" or the acronym "MOS" in referring to themselves?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was an acronym used by us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Used by you.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So the last questions I would have to put -- would like to put on this question is: In this meeting with the Mujahedin, did you have observe any uniforms or Arabic clothes, or could you give a description of their clothes and their appearance.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can recall, this group was in Arabic clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Arabic clothes.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe there have been a mix of uniforms and Arabic clothes, but it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah. You don't recall this quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite clearly after all these years, but I can remember that it was a group of Mujahedins and that the local BiH commander had serious problems to get them away from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My final question: Did you observe any badges or insignia on their clothes?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, you said in response to a question put to you by the Prosecution that you assumed your duties in March, June as part of this European mission. You said that you were a captain in the Danish Army at the time and that you were involved in intelligence. When you were sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina, what were the criteria used when you were recruited? It was as an intelligence officer? Was it in that capacity that you were recruited? Why were you selected? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not selected for that mission. At that time, the Danish Army asked for officers who volunteered, wanted to go to Bosnia or to the Balkans. And when I was sent to the Balkans, I didn't know that I had to go to Bosnia. I learned that the first day when we arrived to the ECMM headquarters in Zagreb. In Zagreb -- the headquarters in Zagreb decided where the new monitors had to be deployed. Then after a few days, I was deployed to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that in Zenica you were in a structure -- you were part of a structure that included Mr. Thebault, there was a Spaniard, there was a German, and you also said that there were Canadian monitors. The Canadian monitor whose name you have provided, Remi Landry, was he part of the mission or was he a monitor within some other body?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remi Landry was a member of the ECMM and he was a monitor as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But this was a European mission; it wasn't a Canadian one. How do you explain this contradiction?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the European Community Monitoring Mission was established, members of the OCE countries were invited to participate. Therefore, countries like Canada, Sweden, Poland, Czechoslovakia participated in the mission, sending monitors to that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The text that the Defence provides us with, it was signed in Sarajevo on the 1st of October, 1991 and it concerned this mission. This text states that the mission was a European one; it was functioning under the European flag. Nevertheless, there were other countries that were included in the mission, other non-European countries. That is what you are telling us. It mentions the flag in Article 5 and further on. There's a lengthy text about this. So there were non-European countries included in the mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as the so-called Totic case is concerned, you said that you were situated in the Hotel Internacional, which is where your mission had its headquarters.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the day that two Mujahedin representatives arrived at the Hotel Internacional, were you present?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the hotel that day. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you see them? Did you personally see them?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall if I saw them when they arrived or I have heard about it, because it's 11 years ago; it's very difficult to remember all the details. But I can remember that I have seen the Mujahedins at the hotel, but I cannot recall if I saw them the very first day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when they were in the hotel, were they armed or did they not have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally they were armed when they arrived, and that's why we had a police guard, a BiH police guard in front of the hotel, so people who were going to visit us were disarmed. But every time the Mujahedins arrived to our hotel, this guard disappeared. But we told the Mujahedins that we didn't want them to have arms when they were visiting us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that the Hotel Internacional was protected by the BiH, given that there were guards who maintained public order in front of the hotel, and on that day, when the two armed Mujahedin entered the hotel, the guards disappeared.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was the civilian police who was guarding the front, but there was only one police officer at the spot. But it's correct; normally when the Mujahedins came, those policemen were -- we saw they were afraid of the Mujahedins. That was the reason for them to run away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the hotel was under the protection of the civilian police, not the military police. You can make the distinction between the civilian and military police, can't you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were wearing different uniforms, but -- and I can't recall who had the responsibility to our security, if it was the civilian police or the military police. I can remember we had this guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the light of your answers, it appears that when this exchange took place you were personally in Travnik and it was your duty to take charge of the four Croatian officers who had been kidnapped. Can you confirm that you were in Travnik in order to take charge of these four Croatian officers?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was in Travnik, and I received the four HVO officers and I bring them with the armed escort from the British Battalion to General Blaskic's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who handed them over to you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members from the Mujahedins, Arabic-speaking members from the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they handed them over to you?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as you are an intelligence officer, you were certainly able to observe certain details in such a situation. That must have been the first time that you had to confront such a situation, because one isn't present when a prisoner exchange takes place every day. When the prisoners arrived, they were escorted by Mujahedin. Were these Mujahedin armed?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed, and they were arriving in an old civilian truck. And I can recall that the Mujahedin that was waiting at the spot together with me, he was armed as well and he was Arabic-speaking, because when he was communicating with the rest of the Mujahedins, they were using our means of communications and they were using the Arabic language when they were communicating. This Mujahedin was able to speak German, so I had the possibility to make some -- a few short conversations with him. I was able -- normally during, -- or while we were waiting, his face was covered by his Balaclava, and I would like to see if he was Bosnian or he was Arabic. So I started to -- I offered him something to eat and I offered him cigarettes, and after a few hours he took off his Balaclava and took something to eat and some cigarettes. And then I was able to see that he was Arabic. And he spoke only Arabic and German.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you didn't ask him which country he was from?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you said that you spoke to him for several hours. So you had the time to talk about various things. It didn't occur to you to ask him where he was from?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it did, Your Honour, but it was -- as an impartial monitor, as we were, very often we were accused from both parts to spy, so we had to be very carefully when we were together with people not to give them the impression that we were spies, because we were not. We were gathering informations, and we knew that those Mujahedins were from foreign countries. We knew that because when we saw the list of the detained Mujahedins, we could see from which country they were from and it was typical from countries from the Middle East and so it was not necessary to ask what specific country they were from. We knew that they were from the Arabic countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Croatian officers were handed over to you -- when you handed them over, did you discuss the matter with the Croatian officers? Did you discuss the conditions under which they had been kidnapped? Did you interrogate them about what had happened to them and about who had arrested them, about where they had been detained, about whether they had been mistreated? In other words, did you ask them the usual type of questions that one asks under such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our task was not to do that. Our task was just to receive them and immediately bring them to the headquarters. But I'm sure that they afterwards have been interviewed by their own headquarters, but I don't have the result of that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't receive any instructions at your level in order to obtain information about what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. My orders were immediately to -- after the release, to bring them to the HVO headquarters in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question is as follows: You said that it was necessary to be impartial when performing your duties and at one point in time you and the Brother Stipan went to see each other. Why didn't you have an Imam come with you? Why did you only take a member of the clergy, whereas you were in the situation where there were people of various religions? Yet you said that it was necessary for you to be impartial. What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were using Father Stipan, it has nothing to be -- to do with our wish to be impartial. We used Father Stipan because we want the Croat inhabitants to believe us. We thought it would be easier for them if we were using Father Stipan, because they trusted him. Normally we didn't have the same problem when we were going to visit the Muslim inhabitants. The Muslim inhabitants, they trusted us and they trusted the representative from BiH we normally had with us when we were visiting Muslim villages. So there was a little difference between the communications between us and the Croats, and us and the Muslim inhabitants. Normally when we were discussing with the Muslim inhabitants and telling about our fact-findings, normally we had -- if it was during a time in the Busovaca Joint Commission or in a later commission, they believed what we said, they believed what the members of our commission, the members from the BiH were telling them. On the opposite side, they didn't always -- the Croats didn't always believe what the Croat members of our commissions were telling them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that the Muslims had more confidence in you than the Croats, as a general rule.

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have no more questions for you. Does the Prosecution have any additional questions for the witness, in the light of the answers that the witness has provided to the Judges' questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does Defence counsel have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have a couple of questions I would like to ask the witness in order to assist The Chamber to understand the witness's testimony. Further cross-examination by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Good morning. Can you confirm that all the ECMM monitors were all dressed in white, that people actually at times were laughing because you were all dressed in white?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they were laughing, but it's correct we were dressed in white. And it's not the best colour to wear during a war, but it's -- we were dressed in white to show all in the theatre that we were on an unarmed mission, so there could be no confusion that if we were a military unit or not. So that's the reason for us to dress totally in white.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. You beat me to my question, which was the fact that you were not armed. Now, can you also confirm that when you visited sites, if you needed to be escorted it would normally be done by BritBat under the UNPROFOR mission with their Warriors?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct, because it was a very difficult period. We had very difficult working conditions, because very often snipers were shooting at us or other units were shooting at us that were units from HVO and units from BiH and from the Mujahedins. So we were provided with armoured escort from UNPROFOR. Normally in the Lasva area we had escort from BritBat; and in the Visoko-Kakanj area, we had escort from the Canadian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Major, one question concerning during the exchange. You mentioned communications amongst the Mujahedin. You are able to confirm that they used at every post the communications equipment that the ECMM monitors had?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that they spoke Arabic all the time?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I have one last question concerning your visit with Father Stipan. You mentioned in answer to the Presiding Judge that you wanted Father Stipan to accompany you so that the Croats would believe you. Can you confirm that when you say they wanted -- you wanted the Croats to believe you, in terms that what the rumours they had heard about, about all the destruction and the burning and the killing were not true, is that what you wanted the Croats to believe?

utterances.speaker: LARS BAGGESEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and that's the reason for us to bring Father Stipan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't want to forget Mr. Dixon this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions for the witness. I am grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, this concludes your testimony in The Hague. Thank you for having contributed to determining the truth. We wish you a good trip home, and we wish you all the best in your career in the Danish Army. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Ms. Benjamin will be conducting the examination-in-chief. Is the witness available now, Ms. Benjamin?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I believe so, Mr. President. He was supposed to be here from 9.00, so I believe he should be outside. If the usher can kindly ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll wait for the usher to return. While waiting for the witness to arrive, Ms. Benjamin, could you inform me of the amount of time you will need for your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not anticipate that we'll take more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you need one hour, the Defence will have an hour and a half, so we could conclude the hearing of this witness today. Madam Usher, could we have the new witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying. If that's the case, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's okay. You've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. You have to take the solemn declaration before testifying. In order to do so, you need to tell us your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Rudy Gerritsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 9th of May, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were you born and in which country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in the Netherlands, in a place called Meppel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your position? What is the rank that you currently hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a lieutenant colonel in the Dutch Army. I'm working now in the army staff as policy advisor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, over ten years ago, what position did you hold in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was an ECMM monitor in the rank of major of the Dutch Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or national court with regard to what happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I testified already once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where was that? Before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which case did you testify in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a good question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is usually the case, when Judges ask questions. It doesn't matter. As you are used to giving testimony, you know that it is necessary to read out the solemn declaration. Could you please read the text of the solemn declaration out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I would like to give you some guidelines with regard to your testimony. As you already know, you have been called by the Prosecution. First you will be answering questions put to you by Mrs. Benjamin, the representative of the Prosecution, on your right-hand side. After these questions, which shouldn't take more than an hour, the two Defence counsel, on the left-hand side, are also going to ask you questions within the scope of their cross-examination. The cross-examination is carried out in order to check the credibility of your answers given within the scope of the examination-in-chief. Also, the cross-examination serves to support the Defence case. In addition to that, the three Judges in front of you may at any moment put questions to you, either to clarify things or to fill the gaps in your answers. It is a customary procedure that the Trial Chamber puts questions to the witness at the very end of the testimony; however, it may happen that they put questions to you even before that, should a need arise for that. I also have to remind you of the following two things: You have taken the solemn declaration, which means that you shouldn't give a false testimony, because that may be punished. When the witnesses answer questions, they may refuse to answer a question should such an answer incriminate them. In such a case, which is exceptional, the Trial Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question; however, the Trial Chamber will give such a witness some sort of immunity. Since the evidence before this Trial Chamber is oral, we kindly ask you to be as precise and as complete in your answers as possible, because the Trial Chamber does not have any written documents to rely on. The only reliable thing for us is what you're going to say today. And this is how we intend to arrive at the truth. And this is in general terms how your testimony is going to be heard. We have another 15 minutes before the break; therefore, I would like to give the floor to Mrs. Benjamin for her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Lieutenant Colonel. Could you briefly state for the Trial Chamber your training before you became a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, training takes a long time in the army. It starts, the training, in 1972, when I went into the army as an 18 years old soldier. Training has several levels: Just a military training we had to study several years. And one of the things we studied was in the Conventions of Geneva, for instance. I studied most of the times in economics and logistics and military -- typical military studies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And after your training, did you yourself do lectures on the Geneva Conventions to other troops?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were -- there came a time in 1993 when you were deployed to Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I came in Bosnia at the -- I think the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is with reluctance that I interrupt my learned friend at the beginning of the examination-in-chief. We can see that the witness has some papers in front of him. We don't know what those are. Are they some notes or documents? We would like to know what those are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant Colonel, you have some papers in front of you. What are those? Are they notes? What is it? The testimony is oral. We are not allowed to rely on any written documents. What is it that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First I have here some notes which -- I have written tomorrow [sic] to explain some things of my own, of myself, and how the work was done by the ECMM. And this is a document in which is a brief shortage Of my daily reports in Bosnia. And this book are the notes which I made in Bosnia. I had such books with me at that time, field pockets, put in your -- how do you call that -- a suit. And here are also some dates and notes in it for my own. But I can do this without.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. This is what we are going to do: For the time being, can you put these documents aside. Answer the questions without the documents. Should it happen that while answering a question you believe that your answer may be more precise if you refer to your notes, please tell us so. Just say that you don't remember something. But I somehow don't believe that this will happen. You are a young man. I don't think you will have any problems with your memory. But if there is something you don't remember and if you want to refer to your notes, just tell us so and we will deal with that case by case. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Thank you for drawing our attention to that. You see things very clearly and help us, because sometimes from where we sit we can't see those things. Thank you. And Mrs. Benjamin, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you to my colleague. I wasn't aware that the witness had his documents with him. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we stated before the interruption, there came a time when you were deployed to Bosnia. And could you tell us with whom were you deployed there.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: After central briefing in Zenica, I went to Gornji Vakuf, and I was deployed there with a colleague monitor called Skat-Rordam. And the other monitor in Gornji Vakuf was on vacation and his name was -- it was a Canadian. I don't remember his name now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Hauenstein -- Peter Hauenstein. And that were the two colleagues at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We would understand if you can't remember the name, because it's quite a long time. But what I'm asking you is which organisation were you with when you were deployed to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I was a member of the European Monitor Mission. So I was from the European Community and I was dressed in white linen and not armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you for the Trial Chamber state the role of the ECMM in Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The main role was that we were impartial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you state for us your duties as an ECMM monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I had to monitor -- to gather information on humanitarian matters, military matters, economic and political matters by driving around and talking to the authorities and the civilian people and over -- all the people who we met when we were going around in our area of responsibility, which was for me at that time Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us or describe for the Trial Chamber how the teams were organised and how the missions were conducted.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. We were -- the head of the mission for Bosnia was in Zenica, who had several teams deployed all over Bosnia. Some places were rather -- our area of responsibilities were rather big and had several teams. In the place we were, Gornji Vakuf, it was only one team, Victor 2. That was -- that consisted of two monitors, one driver, and one interpreter. We were located at that time at BritBat in Gornji Vakuf. There was a company of British Battalion over there. The company commander from the British Battalion was Graham Binns. We were located there for safety reasons. Most of the teams were living in hotels, but at that time in Gornji Vakuf it wasn't possible. Each day we were driving to the several places in our area of responsibility. Most of the days we visited -- we started at Gornji Vakuf itself, and then we went to Prozor or Bugojno, and when we were first in Prozor, we went after that to Bugojno and sometimes we were all day in Bugojno or Prozor. And it depends on the situation. It was depending on the moment, the situation. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you say that Bugojno and Prozor were basically your areas of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. In the centre of Gornji Vakuf, and Prozor on the other hand and Bugojno in the north. North east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would be the submission -- would the writing of reports and submission of reports one of your daily tasks?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. On these issues, I already stated we have to write every day daily reports, and we sent the daily report to the -- to Zenica. From there it went to Zagreb, and from there the comprehension went to the European Committee and to the main capitals of several countries of the European Committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, could you tell us the exact date that you got to Bugojno -- to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I went to Gornji Vakuf at the 18th of July, and to Bosnia I think it was 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 18th of July, when you arrived, could you tell us exactly what you saw.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: On the 18th of July, I drove from Zenica to Gornji Vakuf. I went to BritBat. I arrived there at approximately, I think, 12.00 or -- yeah, approximately I think 12.00. And it was a quite nice day at the 18th of July, and that afternoon I played volleyball with BritBat. That was in the evening. I heard from the British company commander that fightings were going on at Bugojno and that we will visit Bugojno the next morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th of July, you would have made your first visit to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived -- I went to Bugojno, and while we were driving to Bugojno, we saw that fightings were going on between the Muslims and the Croats. And in the beginning, the fightings were concentrating on Bugojno itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you observe anything in -- in the area of Bugojno, with respect to the houses and civilians?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. There was a war going on, so there were houses burning and fightings were going on; and there was shelling; all the things that happens in a fight. And wounded people and dead people and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you had to describe the firing that went on in one word, how would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Serious fightings -- in one word? It's difficult. But it was just a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on your visit to Bugojno on the 19th, did you get the opportunity to speak with anyone, including civilians?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. At that day, we went to the HQ from BiH, also to the HQ of the Croats. We spoke there to -- we had spoken to, for instance, the BiH, Abdulah Jelic that day. And I'm not sure, but I think Selmo Cikotic as well and a number of the people at the HQ of the Croats. And I also met there the priest from the Croats who was in the HQ in -- from the Croats in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the priest's name?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That was Father Janko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you spoke to members of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to assist the Trial Chamber who in your opinion was in command.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: In my opinion, in command was Selmo Cikotic. Also, I met most of the time Abdulah Jelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to assist us with which unit of the BiH was in Bugojno at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. I can't remember the number and the name. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Hotel Kalin --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The Kalin Hotel, yes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- was that a focal point for you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us why.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslims were on the winning hand in the fightings in Bugojno. And in the beginning of the fight, we were concentrating on military and humanitarian matters. We were evacuating wounded people from Kalin Hotel to better places. So -- and in the basement of that hotel there was a hospital and there were lying there several wounded Croats and Muslims. And we succeeded to evacuate them at a certain time. I don't remember exactly the date. After that -- and there was still a stronghold from the Croats in the top of that building, of Kalin Hotel, and they surrendered at the end of the fightings, almost at the end of the fightings in Bugojno, 25th, 26th, 27th or something of July. After that, we concentrate more not on the military issues but more on the POWs and POW cases and humanitarian matters and political matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your investigations carried out and the reports received, in your opinion, who at the time was the attacking army?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Muslims, the BiH. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to take your -- I'd like to ask you now that very soon after the 19th you would have started your meetings; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We had every day meetings. We always started somewhere to try to speak to somebody. So we always were trying to speak to military commanders. And if they weren't there, we went to the priest or to the Imam or to the civilian authorities. And we always tried to speak to somebody and have meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be no exception for the 23rd of July. You would have had a meeting.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Because that was our task, to talk to people, to gather information. And the 23rd of July, what ...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated to us a while ago that you had daily meetings.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I suppose the same would have been for the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the day.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my question to you is: Could you tell us what transpired on the 23rd of July as a result of the meeting that was held?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: What kind of meeting was held on the 23rd of July? May I look in my notes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the 23rd of July -- do you -- well, maybe I shouldn't ask you that. Is there anything particular about Bugojno on your initial arrival? Did you visit any sites?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I visited the HQs, Kalin Hotel. I visited the POW cages. Maybe that was the case on the 23rd of July, but I'm not sure of the dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So could you tell us, then, if you -- if you can't even remember the date, could you start with the first one that you visited and what you have seen.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The POW cage?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I visited at the end four POW cages, but in the beginning I visited two of them. It was at the high school and at the furniture salon. And there were imprisoned the POWs who I first saw when we -- from that battalion, Croat battalion. And that battalion commander I first saw at -- when I visited a number of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe, Colonel, we could start by talking about the furniture salon first so that we can identify them separately. Let's start with the salon first.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, at the furniture salon was -- at the place -- when I was in front of the hospital and it was on the left side, somewhere. And in the basement, that was in a dark place with POWs in it. When we were in such a place, there was water around and the people weren't -- we couldn't see very well, you know, because it was dark, and there were always, of course, guards around us, so it was difficult to speak freely to the POWs. But we gathered always -- we tried to gather names and wrote them down and handed these names over to the authorities, ICRC, my own authority from ECMM, and we handed them also over. And what we found to the local authorities, for instance, Senad Dautovic, Abdulah Jelic, Selmo Cikotic; and we talked about our experiences with the priests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, may I interrupt you now.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can describe for us the conditions at the furniture salon. And in describing it you mentioned that there were guards. Would you be able to assist us with the ethnic background of the guards?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, the ethnic backgrounds of the guards were, of course, from the BiH, from the Muslims, from the -- sometimes that -- I can't remember from the civil police or from the military police. I think in the beginning it was from the civil police, but I'm not sure. Senad Dautovic, the chief of the POW cages, was from the civil police, but the guards, I am not sure of. When we saw on several occasions the POWs, it was obvious for us that they were treated badly. It was not accordance to the Geneva Conventions. They were beaten and they were frightened. That was clear for us, that they were frightened, but they couldn't speak freely, so we couldn't -- and there was blood, there were bandages and so on. They were lying just on the floor or on -- how do you call these -- where you step along goods, pallets. Yes, pallets. They were sometimes lying on the surface, and there they slept on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you raise these concerns with anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We raised these concerns with Senad Dautovic and with Abdulah Jelic and when we met Selmo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Dautovic and Mr. Jelic, were they members of a particular army?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Jelic was from the BiH, as well as Selmo; and Senad Dautovic was from the civil police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: From Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was wondering if this may be a good time for us to take our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Colonel, just like in the army we have to have some breaks for technical reasons. We shall resume at five to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, for clarification's sake, you have referred to the military body BiH. When you say "the BiH," whom do you mean or which body do you mean? Is it the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Before the interruption, we were at the site of the furniture salon, and you had indicated to the Court the conditions that you had observed at the salon, and you were just about telling us of the meetings that you held with the different parties raising your concerns. Now, could you tell me what were the results of your meetings, with respect to the furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We were always promised that the circumstances would be better and that they would investigate the circumstances. Well, that's mainly it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how many detainees were held at the furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: 60, 80. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be able to give us the ethnic background of these detainees.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: These were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Civilians and military people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Would you say, Colonel, that this particular site, the furniture salon, would you say that that site was a suitable site for detaining prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you explain to us why you came to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, I think all POWs should be in a normal prison and not in a salon with water in it and dark, and not enough toilets and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: And not -- there were not enough sleeping -- there were not -- there were no beds at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion - and I think you stated that for the Court previously - you thought that the Muslims had the upper hand at that time.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time then when the HVO surrendered?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. They surrendered and they left Bugojno, and from the Croats a minority of civilians stayed behind in Bugojno itself. And it was at the end of July that HVO withdraw from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, aside from the furniture salon, did you visit any other prison in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I visited the high school, and I visited another school, an elementary school, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we first start with the Bugojno high school.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe what you saw on your visit.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The high school was to the right from the hospital, more to the old centre of the town. The prisoners, the POWs, were also in a cellar and also in the classrooms from that high school building. And the high school was more or less more suitable for POWs than in comparison with the furniture salon. There I met, for instance, for the second time, the battalion commander from that HVO brigade or battalion who did surrender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many detainees would you say were at the high school? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Approximately, the same number, I think. We didn't saw all POWs at the same time. Or when I visited - also I didn't mention that - but that was later on the POWs in the stadium, football stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. We're going to go one by one.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Each side. So we're at the high school. Now, could you tell me if you received any reports or if you spoke to anyone and you gained any information with respect to the conditions, in particular at the high school.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We got some information from the priest, from Father Janko, about the conditions of the POWs in general, not only the conditions from the prisoners in the high school but also from the conditions of the POWs in the furniture salon and later on in the stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any information with respect to deaths, beatings?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: In the furniture salon at a certain moment the POWs were beaten. That was information we got from Father Janko, if I'm -- yes, I think from Father Janko. And because of the beatings, a prisoner died. I can't recall his name at this moment. But the names are in the notes. And he died after beatings. And at a certain moment the -- at a certain meeting, the BiH declared that the same person was died of because he fled from the prison, and we've got the same name. And we met some of the beaten POWs in the hospital at the day after we got the information that they were beaten. And in the same period the responsibility from the POWs was taken over from Senad Dautovic -- was handed over from Senad Dautovic to a military police commander, security officer, Senad -- I think Senad Handzic. Yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, did you yourself visit the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I visited the hospital and I spoke to the POWs who were lying there and were treated there for their injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe for the Trial Chamber what they looked like to you.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, they were severely beaten. They had all kind of bruises on their bodies. And they also make their statements that they were treated badly and that one of them was died because of the beatings. And I saw three or four of them in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Father Janko, were you able to learn anything with respect to the POWs and the civilians who were detained from Father Janko in your inquiries?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, yes, he had several reports. He was the main focal point for the Croat minority, so everything happened for the Croat minority near the church and there was also a lawyer and they made all kind of statements and handed it over to us and we handed these statements over to -- and also names. And all these things we were gathering. And most of the information we've got from Father Janko. And most of the times he also went with us to certain places, meetings. And he had also from the past influence in the Muslim society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber if the members of the ABiH confirmed to you that there were detention centres held by them in Bugojno and as to how many.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. They stated that there were four at a certain moment. That was the furniture salon, the high school, the elementary school, and after that the football stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we have gone through the furniture salon and the high school. Could you tell us your observations of the elementary school and some of the complaints that you received, please.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. From the elementary school, I can't remember a lot. I've been there. I've -- I saw it in my notes, but it is not in my mind what I saw there and what is circumstances were. You asked me before, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It's lost. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your daily meetings, would you have conveyed your concerns and the reports made to you to the representatives of the army?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us how it was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, they -- improvements would be made in the near future and they would investigate and so on, yes. It was -- that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And over the period of time that you were there, did you observe any improvements?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. No. We didn't visit that much those POW cages. We asked for more, if we were allowed to visit these cages more, but we didn't get in and at a certain moment all the POWs were gathered in the football stadium or were sent over to Zenica, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have said to the Trial Chamber that you tried but you didn't get in. Could you tell us who obstructed the access.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Most of the time I think Senad Dautovic or Abdulah Jelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And coming from which army?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: From the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, could you for the Trial Chamber list the offences, starting with the more serious ones first, that you would have received with respect to the complaints, either from Father Janko or the civilians. Could you please assist us with the type of offences that were reported.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, the beatings, the killings, and the rapes from civilian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: And women who were raped, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you assist us with the ethnic background of the victims, please.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: These were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your line of duty or in your duties, was exchanging of POWs part of your portfolio?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please assist the Trial Chamber as to how the procedure took place.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We didn't succeed in exchanging POWs. We tried to arrange the exchanging of POWs and we have a lot of talks and meetings about that subject, but we didn't succeed to exchange them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the negotiating parties in the exchange?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The ABiH, the civilian police, Senad Dautovic, again; and from the Croat side, Father Janko, and the lawyer and the people around Father Janko. And at a later time, the mayor of Bugojno. Mlaco, I think. Mlaco, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, would you say that the members of the ABiH who were in control, would you say or tell us from your opinion if you think that they were fully informed and fully aware of the situation on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
