utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it -- or could you assist us as to whether in your opinion if anything at all was done with respect to the complaints that were made to them with respect to the treatment that was meted out to the POWs, the civilians, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, that I can't be sure of. Of course, they were fully aware what was happening. And also the change of responsibility at a certain moment is a sign for me that they were thinking about it and what to do. But they weren't telling us the facts. It was just on an -- of such level that they say, "We try to get better circumstances for the civilians so that the robbing and looting and raping is not going on, and for the POWs that they won't be beaten," and so on. I think some way on other, sometimes maybe they also tried to do that. They always made statements that they have to go on with living together after the war. Well. But I didn't see personally any improvements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: At that time, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying, then, that the ABiH army did not take the reports seriously?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I think they take the reports seriously but do not make -- they didn't do with it what we want that they do with it. You know? It's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I think they read and they heard the complaints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nothing was implemented.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Nothing was implemented, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to object to the previous question and the penultimate question. They were leading and this is not allowed in the course of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, would you like to respond to the Defence's objection? The Defence claims that the questions you asked the witness are leading ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I beg to disagree with my learned friend, because earlier on the Colonel did say that the complaints were heard and that nothing was done. And I just wanted to verify further for the Court, hence the reason why the question was asked again. He did say that the reports were made and that they didn't see any action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are saying that there were reports; that is your claim. Could you tell the -- and could you tell the Chamber whether there was any follow-up. The witness said that there wasn't any. That was the meaning of your question, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my learned colleague, with all due respect, has misquoted the witness again, because the witness did not say that they did not do anything. He said that he personally did not see any proof. So I would like to object again to my colleague quoting the witness's testimony in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has taken note of your objections. Ms. Benjamin, will you be continuing with your examination-in-chief or have you concluded now?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, you indicated to the Trial Chamber that you had meetings on a daily basis concerning the situation in Bugojno and that you wrote reports. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber tell us basically the contents of the reports, basically what they would be like.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: In the reports, we wrote the conditions of the -- for instance, of the POWs, the bodies we saw, and the accusations - is that the right word - who were made, who we met, at what time, and what we tried to achieve. We always -- and sometimes we wrote that in a daily report and sometimes when it was more we wrote down in a special report the specific circumstances. We met that day and we also wrote down the names we've got or we wrote down personally from people we met or POWs who we saw. Most of the times we let the -- for instance, the POWs wrote down their own names on papers because it was difficult for us to understand the names because of the difficulty of the difference of language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would by correct in saying that your report basically would contain the humanitarian aspect, the military aspect? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Chamber's permission, I wish to show the witness Exhibit P273, Prosecution Exhibit 273.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant colonel, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, would this be one of the typical reports that would have been written on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 4, it speaks of the humanitarian activity, and you outlined on that particular day all the information that you received. Is this what transpired on a daily basis in all your reports?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you take it back, please. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your period of duty began on the 18th of July, 1993. Could you tell us when it came to an end.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It came to an end at the 12th, I think, or 15th of September. I think the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that a typical day in the life of a colonel during that period was basically writing reports, visiting sites, doing exchanges? That's basically what your tour of duty was all about.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel, in your opinion, was the goals of the ECMM achieved during your tenure, and how successful would you say was your mission?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I think we were interesting for both sides, the Croats and the Muslims, and we handed -- we didn't only pass over information to the capital cities of the European Committee but also we handed over information to both sides; in this case, Croats and Muslims. And I think this was a benefit and a kind of assurance for some people, not for all. And -- yeah, I wouldn't talk about success, you know. It's -- we did our job. I can't find the right words. I can't talk about success. But we did our job. That's mainly it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We tried to do the good thing, you know. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by "success" I meant you were able to make all parties aware of what was going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All parties had full knowledge of what was taking place.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. And they -- we didn't only do it by ourself. They also asked for us. You know, that was also the way we could work there and our kind of life insurance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, in your opinion, who during the period of time that you were there, between the 18th of July and the 12th of September, who in your opinion you would say would have been the aggressor, the main attacker?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning, specifically in Bugojno it was the ABiH. Of course, it was -- there were more attackers than only the ABiH in Bosnia, but we all know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Bugojno -- but Bugojno specifically.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: -- ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Benjamin. I'll now give the floor to Defence so that they can conduct their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Lieutenant Colonel Gerritsen. My name is Edina Residovic, and I represent General Hadzihasanovic, together with my colleague Stephane Bourgon and Alexis Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in addition to the questions that arise from the questions put by my learned colleague Ms. Benjamin, I would like to ask the witness some questions of a general kind, since the witness was present in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps at the time in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, you said that you have already testified before this Tribunal in another case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may remind you, that was in the Kordic and Cerkez case and you had been called as a witness for the Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you gave the OTP a statement on two occasions. The first time was on the 20th of March and on the 9th -- and the second time, on the 9th of April, 2002. On those occasions, you discussed the BH army, and on the 25th of April and the 5th of May, 2002 you discussed the HVO in greater length. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave these statements, you were already aware of the fact that the generals from the Bosnian army had been indicted by the International Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you have already told my learned colleague, in July 1993 you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina and you joined the European Monitoring Mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First you arrived in Zenica in the regional centre in which the head of the centre was a Frenchman, Jean-Pierre Thebault. He decided to sent you to the team which was deployed in Gornji Vakuf. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason why you were sent to Gornji Vakuf was the deterioration of relationships between the BiH army and the Croatian Defence Council in Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your testimony, you arrived in Gornji Vakuf on the 18th of July, 1993 and you joined the monitoring team V2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In keeping with the rules of the European monitors, every day you would draft a report on what you had personally seen, on the meetings that you had as well as on the information that you had received, and you would dispatch these reports to the regional centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a free agent in drafting these reports. You were under no pressure to record the things that you didn't hear or didn't see yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these regular daily reports and based on these reports, the regional centre would draft their own overviews of the situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would happen that some very important issues would be covered in special reports drafted by the head of the mission. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It seems logical to me. But I didn't see any of these reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You arrived in Gornji Vakuf on the eve of major conflicts between the BiH army and the HVO in Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of that, the situation in the region was not well known to you; however, subsequently you were informed by your colleagues about the events that preceded those conflicts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your own words, within the scope of your mission you met a number of persons that belonged to both the military and the civilian authorities as well as some officials that were important for the work of the community, like religious officials and political figures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the tour of your duty, you never met General Hadzihasanovic. You didn't know what position he held at the time. Would I be correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your mission, you didn't meet any other members of the 3rd Corps staff which was located in Zenica; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. In Zenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never sent any written information about what you saw in the command of the 3rd Corps; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the very beginning, you learnt that Bugojno was in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps and that the Operative Group West units were operational in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were talking about the things that you learnt during your mission and the preceding events, would it be correct that at the time you learnt that the area of Prozor, Gornji Vakuf was the area of constant fights from the very beginning of the conflict between the army and the HVO, that is, October 1992; and this continued throughout January 1993, February 1993, throughout the duration of your mission? Is that something that you learnt while you were there?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I'm looking for the dates. Oh, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also learnt that as a result of these attacks by the HVO on Vakuf -- Gornji Vakuf and Prozor many Muslims from the surrounding neighbouring villages were either expelled from the area or detained or even killed. Did you become aware of that fact as well?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the duration of your mission there was fighting in Gornji Vakuf and the front line went through the centre of that town; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also informed that the HVO and the BiH army before your arrival cooperated in Bugojno and that they manned the defence lines together and that they fought together against the Serb forces. Did you also learn that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also learnt that in the course of 1993 tens of thousands of refugees came to the area when they were expelled by the Serbs from the area of Krajina and Donji Vakuf; were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also knew that the town of Bugojno was regularly shelled from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could also hear from your colleagues that in mid-July the HVO withdrew their units from the defence lines facing the Serbs, which created a lot of problems because one part of the territory was surrendered to the Army of Republika Srpska. And as for the rest of the positions, the BiH army had to invest a lot more effort in order to keep those lines.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I think, for me, this was one of the theories. I am familiar with that statement, but it's not a certain yes that this was the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the moment of your arrival, your mission had already had a lot of evidence about cooperation between the HVO and the Army of Republika Srpska against the BiH army. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: They even helped the refugees, the Serbs, yes. There were always cooperations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you could see and what you learnt told you that the HVO was much better armed, they had heavy weapons, whereas the BiH army had more troops. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was my opinion, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that, the HVO had a flow of weapons from Western Herzegovina and Croatia, whereas the BiH army had a total embargo on the import of any kind of weapons into the area; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That is also a statement which I can't confirm personally. That was one of the main lines at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO brigade which fought in the area of Gornji Vakuf did not belong to the Operation Zone Central Bosnia, they belonged to the Operation Zone North-western Bosnia and their commander was Commander Siljeg -- correction, North-western Herzegovina and the commander was Commander Siljeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your mission was aware of the fact that in that area a lot of troops came from Herzegovina and a lot of the troops also belonged to the Croatian army. Were you aware of that fact? Could you that with your own eyes as a member of the mission?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We would be always trying to gather that information if that were troops right from Croatia. We couldn't confirm that. But it seems logical to us at that time, but we couldn't see the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct that the HVO carried out, in sense, operations in order to occupy Gornji Vakuf because Gornji Vakuf was on one of the main roads and this would serve to cut Central Bosnia from the arrival of any goods or anything that could serve for their survival?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Both parties had the same interest, because there were also pockets more in the central region of Bosnia from the Croats, and they were also cut off from the supplies from the south to the north. And that's certainly the reason that Gornji Vakuf was a very important place in the routes -- in supply routes to the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of the importance of the main roads, the European monitors placed a lot of emphasis on that issue. That's why I would kindly ask you to look at the special report that the Ambassador Thebault drafted in that respect. My question will be as follows: Would that be the kind of report that the European Monitoring Mission would draft covering important issues in the area?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be provided with this document. We have a sufficient number of copies for everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, do you believe that this was one of those major issues and that you personally witnessed efforts to put a special emphasis on that issue?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it's the main issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is an official document drafted by the head of the European Monitoring Mission. And since the witness is aware of the fact that this covers an important issue, we would like to tender this report into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Registrar, can we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be DH169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, from the reports, you were able to learn that both the BiH army and the civilian authorities of Bugojno tried to deal with every problem in a peaceful way. Were you informed about that from your colleagues, and could you learn that from the reports?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Before I came in, there were meetings - I've learned that from my colleagues - where they tried to go on in a peaceful way and to be a community as was before. There were several meetings on that subject, and there were also several incidents who made the progress in these meetings difficult. But I'm not aware of these incidents because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could also learn that in mid-July tensions in the town itself intensified, tensions between the BiH army and the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The direct information that you received about the beginning of the conflict spoke about the checkpoint at the crossroads leading towards the Croatian village of Kandija. The checkpoint was set up by the HVO. This is where the fighting started, when Bosniak population was ill-treated. A checkpoint was then set up by the BiH army. The conflict spread onto that checkpoint, and two Croatian members of the HVO were killed there. Are you familiar with all that? Are you familiar with that incident?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that very day, the 17th of July, the MUP of Bugojno and the HVO police formed a joint patrol consisting of four Muslims and four Croats. Their task was to go to the crime scene and establish why the incident happened. The HVO attacked the patrol, killed three Bosniaks, and one managed to escape. Is this the information that you received about the incident at this checkpoint not far from the village of Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, not in this detail. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you must have learnt that after that the HVO attacked the village of Vrbanja and that this conflict at the checkpoint near Vrbanja spread on, to the town of Vrbanja -- on to the town of Bugojno? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, there were several theories about -- for the beginning of the fight, and... Well, I can't confirm if this was really the one, you know? But that's my problem, because I didn't get all these informations. Even now I haven't them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why you cannot confirm that the BiH army attacked Bugojno; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I would say that the beginning of the fights and why the fights started, I cannot confirm. But that the BiH was attacking Bugojno and expelling the Croats, that's what I confirmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can confirm, however, that at the moment when the fighting spread onto the town, the commander of the Operation Zone West was not in the town; he was in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The commanders have their communications, and they are not always on the front line. That's correct. So he could be in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an officer, you know that it would be normal if a town or the main town is being attacked in his area of responsibility in the Operation Zone West, that it would be normal for a commander to be in his area of responsibility, rather than several hundreds of kilometres away from that zone. In your capacity as an officer in the army, would you not say that this would be a normal procedure?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It depends on which level the commander is. There are several levels, you know, and I can't -- I haven't a clue of -- on which level this commander you are talking about now was at that moment. I only dealt with the people over there on the ground, and the highest one from the Muslim side I saw at that moment was Selmo Cikotic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was Selmo Cikotic who wasn't in the town at the beginning of the fighting in town. He appeared maybe two or three days later.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's -- for me is strange, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This fact would also confirm that if Selmo Cikotic was not in the area, he could not have planned or he could not have started the fighting; that this fighting spread spontaneously after the incident that happened one or two days before at the checkpoint that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have testified that on the 19th of July you attempted to enter the town but you failed due to the heavy fighting that was taking place in the town itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The 19th of July was on a Monday, and on Monday we were in Bugojno. In the afternoon. Because -- we didn't succeed in the morning of a broke-down armoured vehicle from BritBat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, the fighting in town was so heavy that it did not lend -- the town did not lend itself as an area for negotiations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. At that day we went to the HQ from ABiH and we asked for the situation and so on, and we also went to the HQ from the HVO. But we didn't negotiate about a peace settlement or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A lot of the Croatian population from the town together with the HVO unit withdrew through the Serbian territory because they did not want to accept the invitation of the Bugojno authorities to return and to live together. Were you aware of that fact? Did you witness that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't witness the flee through Serb territory, but we heard several times about that and I spoke to several people about that certain event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict, your contacts were mostly with the civilian authorities in Bugojno, in particular with the chief of the civilian police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Also, also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your main task throughout this fighting was to care for the wounded who were at the Kalin Hotel, the wounded belonging both to the BiH army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first thing you learnt from the representatives of the army on the 23rd of July was that a massacre had taken place in a cellar. Three Muslims had been massacred by the HVO. Together with the representatives of the BiH army and the doctor from the BritBat, you went to that cellar to see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You found three persons who had been tortured, who had been disfigured, and a lady doctor from the BritBat drafted a report on your findings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. She made a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your return, you saw some detainees from the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade of the HVO. You were given an opportunity to talk to talk to them. They told you that they were treated well. You took their names, and nobody prevented you from doing that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. After insisting to talk with them, we were allowed to talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were informed that between 300 and 500 members of the HVO were detained. On the 27th of July, you asked to be allowed access to the prison. This was given to you on the 28th of July, when you visited the Gimnazija and the furniture store. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went there, and after that you drafted a report on what you had seen and how many detainees you had seen at those two places; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th of July, you reported about the beginning of the conflict in Bugojno, and on the 23rd of July you filed a report on having found three dead civilians in the basement. On the 25th of July, you described your humanitarian activities when providing wounded HVO members with assistance; and on the 26th, your report mentioned the fact that the HVO had used in Livno a bomb against Muslim civilian facilities. Is that the manner in which you filed daily reports?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. The Livno bombs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask the witness to have a look at part -- at some of the daily reports from July. He drafted these reports, and I would like to show them to him in order to be able to ask him some questions. Mr. President, we have a series of nine reports. This forms one bundle. And we would like the documents to be admitted into evidence under one number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have not the -- on the screen, not the right -- oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has eleven reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These reports are from the month of July, after the witness had arrived in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nine or eleven reports? Because the transcript says "11 reports." Do we have nine or eleven reports?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have nine for the month of July, and later the Defence will also show the witness some reports from August. But we would like these reports, providing that the witness recognises them, be accepted as one piece of evidence. Could the reports please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these reports that you yourself drafted, either on an independent basis or working together with your colleague?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Working together with my colleague. Some were written by me, by myself, and some by my colleague. It depends on where we were and how tired we were and so on. But most of the time my colleague, who was Peter Hauenstein, who was a Canadian guy, and he wrote better English. So he always checked my reports, if I had wrote down in correct English our information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to say that in this bundle of reports there are probably two reports for the 28th of July, because we received the same reports that had different numbers. We therefore copied both reports, in spite of the fact that they are identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you have a look at your report dated the 28th of July. Could you have a look at item 4 --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 28th.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I have two of them. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at them. They are identical, but the numbers they've been given are different. I have just explained to the Trial Chamber why we have two identical reports. Could you have a look at item 4 in this report. Does it state that on that day you visited the detainees in the Gimnazija, in the secondary school? There were 152 of them and there were 94 detainees in the furniture salon, in the furniture showroom. It also states that it seems that they were being detained in good conditions. It also states that there were certain deficiencies, certain shortcomings, and it says that on the following day you will visit other facilities in which detainees are kept in the town. You also said that you would suggest that the Red Cross make it possible for the detainees to be provided with essential supplies. Is that what you reported with regard to this visit?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't mention any bad conditions in the report. You didn't mention the conditions that you have testified about today before this Court.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The basic conditions in the high school were better than in the furniture salon. As I can recall, in the furniture salon were no beds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, and it's the same item, you stated that you had discovered that 40 Muslim civilians were being held by the HVO. You said that they were being very badly treated, that there were old people and children among them, and you stated that it was obvious that they had been maltreated and that after your first visit, when you returned, you discovered that they had been maltreated again. Is that what you reported?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, that's -- I must -- oh, yes, the visit to a young woman. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You found out from those people that before your visit one of the detainees was killed. Did you find out about that fact?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Which detainee? From the 40 Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, I can't recall that. We spoke to the three women at a certain time who were held apart from the 40 -- from the others who were in the cellar of the later torched hotel. I do not remember that somebody was killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back to another subject. It's not mentioned in the report, but I would like to ask you about this matter to see if you can remember anything about it. In fact, the 40 Bosniak civilians, the women, the children, and the old people, you managed to exchange them for 23 wounded Croats who were being treated in the Bugojno hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now have a look at your report dated the 29th of July. Under item 4, "Humanitarian activity," you stated that you had visited -- I apologise. This is a report in which your visit to the school is being mentioned again. I apologise. Perhaps I have the wrong document. Is it the same document? It relates the same facts that were mentioned on the 28th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they do. That seems to be strange, isn't it? Because it's the same -- it's exactly same as the 28th. That seems strange to me, but ... There's something gone wrong, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are your reports. We received them from the ECMM. Perhaps given that the periods when you filed these reports are different, perhaps you reported on the same situation. Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think they are mixed one way or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the report dated the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Wait. This is -- the 29th?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The date is the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I have two reports now, from the 29th as well. One is the same as from the 28th, and one is a different one. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Do you see this -- 29th, 29th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at this number, 1712150206201 is the ERN number. Do you have that number? It says R0206201. Do you have that report?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under item 4 in this report, you stated that you had visited the primary school in Bugojno and that there were 90 detainees there, including soldiers and they were probably people between 40 and 60 years of age, and you said that they were being treated correctly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw HVO soldiers here too and they had been detained there. They were either HVO soldiers or members of the Home Guards. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: At which place? It's going too quick now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's under item 4.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Item 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second sentence. It says: "There were 90 prisoners with a mixture of soldiers from the 1st Battalion and from the Home Defence."

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stated that they were being treated correctly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the report dated the 31st of July. Under item 4.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that you had seen some detainees digging graves, and on that occasion you saw three dead bodies and the Muslims who were there said that this was a massacre that had been carried out by the HVO and that there were another 20 such bodies. You said that these people had been dead for a week. Is that what you stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I have -- yes. But we didn't see the 20 others. Okay, that's what the report stated. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, given that the witness has recognised all the reports shown to him and has said that he himself drafted these reports or did so together with his colleague and he has commented on a certain number of these reports, I suggest that these documents be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before hearing what Ms. Benjamin has to say, all these documents mention Rule 62. So when these documents were sent to you, you were told that these documents shouldn't be disclosed outside the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you discussed the issue of Rule 70 with the European mission? It's Rule 70 and not 62.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you were able to follow our exchanges with the European Community, and you know that this problem was finally dealt with by the OTP. They solved the problem. And after the OTP was given permission to disclose these documents to the Defence to be used in court, the OTP then provided us with the documents in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, could you confirm that that is what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is certainly correct, what my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence just informed you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber wanted to remind everyone of this, to ensure that everything was clear. As far as this request to have these documents admitted into evidence, are there any objections to be raised by the Prosecution? The witness has recognised the documents that he himself drafted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number -- one exhibit number for this bundle of nine reports.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit number for the bundle will be DH170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may continue. We have another seven minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown ten daily reports drafted by the witness in August, as I would like to ask the witness some questions about the reports. And I would like to say that within this bundle of ten documents there are two documents and we have a number of copies of the same document. The reason is the same for this: We were provided with these documents by the Prosecution. And there's also a document dated the 5th of August, 1993. It's P305. And there is a document dated the 10th of August; I think the exhibit number is P273. We will show these documents to the witness now to hear his comments because we will later withdraw them from this series of documents and we will tender this bundle of documents as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, could you now have a look at the document dated the 5th of August. You had a look at it a minute ago when my learned colleague, Ms. Benjamin, was examining you. Under item 1, paragraph 3 you stated that you had already seen civilians in the street at that time and you said that you had a meeting with the president of the War Presidency, with the UNHCR representatives, with the chief of the civilian police, and with representatives of Croats in Bugojno. You discussed the subject of humanitarian aid. You discussed organising Croatian civilians and their committees. And you also discussed the subject of prisoners of war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Representatives of the civilian authorities and of the police informed you on that occasion that sometimes prisoners were beaten. They also informed you that one detainee had been killed because he had attempted to flee. But most importantly, they informed you that as of that time the army would take over responsibility for the prisons and prisoners. That was stated in item 4 of your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting, the authorities in Bugojno said that they were ready for the Croatian population to join the organs of power and said that they were ready to deal with their problems and solve their problems. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now have a look at your report of the 9th of August. Would it be correct to say that on that day you also spoke to representatives of various organs from Bugojno and on that occasion you were informed that 98 per cent of the civilians who had been brought in were released after a brief interview and you also were told that others would soon be released? You were also told on that occasion that the town stadium would be used as a place where all detainees would be kept so that detainees would be held only in the stadium and the primary school. Is that the gist of the conversation that you had with the representatives of the civilian authorities in Bugojno on that day?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that on that occasion you were told that there were serious problems as far as food was concerned and other essential items, such as items for hygiene, medical supplies, and they asked for the UNHCR to help in order to solve these problems? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gained the impression that the authorities wanted to do everything they could in order to improve the conditions but there were many difficulties they had to face and there was a shortage of the most essential items that are necessary in order to survive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I gained the impression that the authorities wanted to do everything. I think that's -- I'm not so sure about that, you know, that they had really the intention. It is more saying -- it is more a political statement, in my impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you are aware of the fact that at the time there was no water in Bugojno because the HVO in areas that were under its control cut off the water supply to the town. They cut off the supply for the population and for the detainees. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We heard about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you and UNPROFOR, together with the HVO and the Croatian authorities in the territory under their control, attempted to solve the problem, but the Croatian authorities in the HVO refused to cooperate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I think the subject is right, but I can't recall a hundred per cent from the Croatian -- the statement of the Croatian authorities and the HVO. I was not at that meeting, I think, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, on the basis of your personal experience, were you aware of the fact that there wasn't enough food and there weren't enough medical supplies in the town and the UNHCR and the Red Cross had to supply a minimum of these necessities to make it possible for people to survive. Regardless of what is stated in the report, is this something that you are aware of on the basis of your personal experience in that area at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, there was a lack of everything, of course. And we tried to bring in aid from UNHCR, ICRC, but at that time they were not allowed to bring the aid in because it was too dangerous. We didn't -- I'm not sure about that, if we have had the permission to bring all this aid in, in a way that ICRC and UNHCR were -- could be bring in the aid safely. You know. There must be some assurances from both parties when UNHCR and ICRC get in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have testified--

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question, Mr. President, and then we will be ready for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have said that what you saw when visiting the prisons was not entirely in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. My question is as follows: What you saw, was it exactly what could have been provided for the prisoners of war under the given conditions?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I think we should ask that to the military commanders. There are always lines of communications and lines to supply. And if -- that was the theory we had at that time. If the military people can get food, then the POWs or civilians should have the same amount of supplies, you know. But we didn't know all supply routes. So it's just theory for us what was possible or not possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will be ready to continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to need another 15 minutes or so for my -- for the rest of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Are you going to ask for these ten documents to be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I would -- before that, I would like to discuss a few of the other documents with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We shall now take a break until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, before the break, we were talking about various shortages and the request by the civilian authorities for assistance which would enable them to provide better conditions both for the prisoners of war and the civilian population. In order to deal with this huge problem, the civilian authorities allowed Caritas to help with providing the prisoners. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. No. I'm not sure of that. This is kind of familiar, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name of Sister Pavka, who was a member of the Caritas organisation?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Sister Pavka one of those who were allowed to visit prisoners and bring food to them? Are you aware of that fact? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that. I met Sister Pavka in the Kalin Hotel, and after that twice in Kandija, I think, and in Split. But not for this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that families could also bring food to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that the prisoners were provided with medical care, that a lady doctor visited them, and also that prisoners who were hospitalised in the hospital in Bugojno were treated in the same way as any other patient?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that was stated many times. What I saw in the hospital, I will -- I have to confirm this. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, Lieutenant Colonel, that the representatives of the Croatian people informed you on the 17th of August about 18 crimes against Croats - among them rapes, robberies - and that they provided you with a list that you gave to the chief of the Bugojno police at a meeting which took place on the following day, on the 18th of August?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at the report of 18 August, please. On that day, there was a meeting with the representatives of authorities in Bugojno and representatives of the Croatian people. You discussed the political situation, and they told you what the plan was for helping their fellow citizens who were a minority at that time. Was that a subject matter of your discussion at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in Bugojno, out of the 16.000 employed before the war, there were only 2.000 people who held a job and that the most difficult thing for the Croatian population of Bugojno was that there were no jobs, that they couldn't find work?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay. It's stated here, but it's not a subject for me. I have -- I didn't any investigations on that subject. That's better to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall now move on to your report dated 19 August. I would kindly ask you to look at item 4. Is it correct, Lieutenant Colonel, that you reported that on that day, together with the chief of police, you inspected in great detail the list containing 18 names of civilians that was given to you by the Croats, indicating a number of grave crimes against the Croatian population; and that on that occasion you were provided with detailed information about the actions that had been taken by the police, that two people had already been arrested, some investigation was underway, that in three or four cases the deaths were not due to crimes but rather to shelling? Is it true that you spoke in such a great detail about the list that you gave to the chief of police on that day?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware of the fact that the state authorities took their job very seriously and that they accepted your suggestions and they accepted the facts that you presented them with and that they were trying to carry out investigation despite the fact that it was sometimes very difficult to know who the perpetrators were -- is that what you were told at the meeting with the representatives of the authorities on that day?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that such is stated here. I'm more -- I would like to say that what I was thinking at that time and also now, that that's the question, you know. Have they done enough investigations and so on and so on? Is it true what they say? It was a statement from the civil police and -- well, that's it. It is not my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to put to you that the procedures were carried out before international courts of law, then the statement that you were -- that you heard then from the chief of police would appear to be correct; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. I can't say it is true or not true, because I couldn't do any investigations by myself and I had to rely on their statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have testified that an issue of exchange of prisoners was raised. Is it true that the president of the War Presidency and the civilian authorities informed you initially that all the prisoners of war would be transferred to the detention facility in Zenica where the centre for POWs was? Is it true that you received this information?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I've got that information. But -- I've got it from the -- I think from Dautovic, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also know that on the following day, when this transfer was supposed to take place, this wasn't carried out because there was not enough buses.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the reason that they gave you for not transferring people? Are you aware of the fact that after that, representatives of the Croatian people, together with a lawyer who worked as a member of that committee, asked for the civilian authorities and the court in Zenica for the prisoners not to be transferred to Zenica but, rather, for them to stay in Bugojno and if a trial should be carried out, they should be tried in Bugojno, because they were afraid that something could happen to them on the way from Bugojno to Zenica? Are you aware of all this?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, not in this detail. No. The buses, I remember, but not this. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have also testified about your discussions on exchange. However, while you were there, there was no exchange carried out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The local authorities, both military and civilians, told you that this issue was being dealt with at a higher level of authority. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, I think that's correct. I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that at that time an agreement was signed between the Bosnian-Herzegovinian government, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Croatia and the HVO, that there would be an exchange of all the prisoners involving the POWs from Bugojno and some other prisoners and the prisoners held by the HVO in Mostar, Ljubuski, and elsewhere? Are you aware of the fact that such agreement was indeed signed?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that if at the level of the heads of state such an agreement had been signed, that then commanders at a lower level were not in the position to act independently and make independent decisions on any of the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I do not agree with that. But that's the way we are working in the Dutch Army. We always think that the people who are at the newest spot, at the centre of an event, they could decide the best for these kind of things, you know. And we don't like all these higher levels. So I would decide -- I could decide something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Lieutenant Colonel, since you have answered a number of questions put to you both by the Prosecution and myself, would you agree with me that if there is a difference between what you have said today and what is stated in the documents that you drafted in 1993, then that what you drafted in 1993 would be correct? Because the lapse of time may have had an influence on you forgetting some of the things that happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that's always a possibility. But there are also other explanations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my cross-examination, and now could I please have an exhibit number for this bundle of documents which have been drafted by the witness and the witness himself has been able to provide comments for all of these documents drafted in August 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have a number for these ten documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number will be DH170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any cross-examination by the other Defence counsel, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am turning towards Mrs. Benjamin. Any re-examination which might arise from the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Re-examined by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, a while ago -- page 8, line 7 -- rather, line 1, my colleague suggested to you that with the passage of time you may have forgotten some of the incidents, and hence the reason why the statements in your reports are different to some of your testimony here today. And you replied by saying, Yes, but that there were also -- that's a possibility, but there were also explanations. And could you explain to the Trial Chamber the other explanations for us, please.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. And my memory when I look to the results, there were beatings and POWs were badly treated. And POWs were killed. At least from one we know for sure -- I know for sure. When we visited with -- with allowance from the local authorities, when we visited POWs, it's obvious that there will be preparations to show the best. And when I look as a whole to what I've seen and after so many years what I have in my memory but -- then my conclusion is that they are not treated in accordance to the Geneva Conventions. But I also agree with the Defender that after so many years memories are mixed up. So I'll think both interpretations are possible. Well -- and my memory and my opinion is not the truth, that it's -- it's not the only truth, you know. That's the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. And in my colleague's cross-examination, she alluded to the fact of the refugees and the Serbs coming into Bugojno. Would you agree with me that the new demographic condition of Bugojno caused great discomfort and was of great detriment to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that some of those very refugees that she talked about are responsible for some of the atrocities that were brought upon the Croats at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you help the Court with perhaps at least one group of refugees who you would have known that would have caused these atrocities?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I must go to my files here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was hoping that we would not have had to go for that. You were doing pretty well.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me help you, if I may.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My colleague spoke to you about the Serbs that came in. And did you see any other foreigners, so to speak, in Bugojno at the time, other than the -- the natives, foreigners? Did you see any other refugees?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. I saw -- yeah, not the refugees--

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I saw Arab people, but that is not a refugee for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Stop, please. Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what my learned friend implied, but I have never spoken about any Serbs that arrived in the city. Serbs resided in Bugojno. I never mentioned Serbs, save for the Serbian army that shelled Bugojno. I don't believe that my learned friend should be allowed to raise that question based on my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, the Defence says that they have never mentioned the Serb refugees, the Serb arrivals. Why did you ask this additional question which was not addressed during the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I stand corrected. But I was under the impression that when my learned friend was talking about the demographic conditions, she spoke about other armies, the Serbs being in there, other people coming into the Bugojno area. And I think that's when the witness answered yes, it wasn't only the ABiH; it was other armies as well. And that is the vein in which the question is asked, because it wasn't only the Serbs, it was other armies as well. That was the question. And he quite rightly answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was more on the front lines. These things are...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. And before you were interrupted, your mind -- you had a recollection and you said that they looked like Arabs. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. But that was after the fightings. I only saw one Arab people, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you saw one Arab.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's not the Mujahedin who everybody is searching for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And one final question: What is your opinion of -- what do you consider as to be "treated correctly"? Could you give a definition for the Court what you consider to be "treated correctly."

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We should look in the Bible, I think. "Treated correctly" is -- you should treat somebody as you wish you were treated yourself, you know. That's "treated correctly."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So if I give you one meal a day, am I treating you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, everybody here, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I lock you up against your will, am I treating you correctly, from holding you --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Against my will, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I treating you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, no, of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant Colonel, the Judges would also like to put some questions to you. I'm giving the floor to the Judge on my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any issues to raise after the re-examination? If not, then there will be a question by the Judge. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant Colonel, you have told us that you visited the detention centres. My question to you is as follows: Who was in charge? Who was standing guard in those detention centres that you visited?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I think the civil police at the beginning, and at a certain moment the responsibility was shifted to the military police. But after that, as far as I can recall, I didn't visit the POW cages any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. However, when you visited those detention centres, did you not want to put any questions to the detainees? Did you not want to discuss things with them?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, we -- we did. But the responsibility, we always spoke with Senad Dautovic. In my opinion, he was responsible as a whole for the prisoners and he was, of course, guided one way or another. Well, that's mainly it. And everybody had -- there were civilians who were guarding and there were also people who were in a kind of military uniform. But the military uniforms at that time were very different. You know, not everybody had the same uniform. So it is difficult to say if only civil police was there or military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, in addition to the civil or military police, you didn't see anybody else? There was nobody else there?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, not for guarding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant Colonel, to follow up on the questions that you have just heard. You visited these two detention centres as a European monitor in your capacity as a representative of the European Union. You went to those detention centres. You have told us that you spoke to Mr. Senad Dautovic, who was a civilian representative, and you have also stated that there were military prisoners, prisoners who were soldiers. And an officer with your rank obviously can make a distinction between a civilian and a soldier. Those were then troops under the control of the civilian authorities. At that moment you should have spoken to the civilian authorities. Did you not ask yourself that question?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. We spoke to both. We also had our meetings with Abdulah Jelic about this subject. And as far as I can remember now, for the definitive visit to POW, we always were guided at that specific day from the visit to Dautovic and not from the headquarters of the BiH, but I'm not sure about that. Yeah. It's hard to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You visited together with Mr. Dautovic the premises, the facilities, and you saw the detainees there. You didn't ask Mr. Dautovic the reason for which they were detained? Because as you are well aware, in all democratic countries if someone is detained, this can only be done on the basis of laws; otherwise, their detention is totally arbitrary. You didn't ask Mr. Dautovic why these detainees were being held there? In spite of the fact that this was the essential task you had, this was what your mission involved. You were there in order to file daily reports about the situation, in spite of the fact that one might ask what the purpose of certain paragraphs is. You had to report on the general situation, the political situation, the military activities; on the other hand, you were involved in humanitarian activity. But in spite of all of these facts, you didn't ask him such a question. What could you tell us about the situation these people were in, these people who were apparently being held there by the civilian police, although there were members of the military who were present? One would have expected that you would ask Mr. Dautovic about the situation in which these people found themselves. That would have been the least one should have done.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, what I stated was that in my opinion it was the civilian police, but that it also could be members of the military police. And I stated something about the different uniforms. I agree with you, Mr. President, that I should have asked those questions, which I didn't. That's the only thing I can say about that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a document shown by the Defence, you filed a report on the 5th of August. This document states in paragraph 4, which concerns humanitarian activity, that there was a total of 3 to 4 hundred prisoners. This is an enormous number. But at the end of the paragraph you say that "The Croatian representative has a list mentioning 2.500 Croats allegedly detained in Bugojno after the conflict, after the fighting." This is something contained in a document you drafted. You said there were over 300 and the Croatian representative said there were 2.500, and your report doesn't comment on this difference, as far as the numbers are concerned. Nothing is said about this. In paragraph 9, it mentions the intentions for future action. Didn't you feel it necessary to try and clarify the difference as far as the official number of detainees was concerned, 3 or 4 hundred detainees, and the other number that appeared, namely 2.500 Croats? Didn't you want to see why there was such a difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. The witness doesn't have the document before him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's no problem. I can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can remember it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Need to explain. The 2.500 is the correct minority which stayed behind in Bugojno, and they weren't imprisoned. They were in their houses and they were kind of detained in Bugojno. They weren't allowed to go to Prozor or to Gornji Vakuf. And the 3 to 4 hundred detainee, they were imprisoned and they were the POWs, and that was a total of the four or seven or whatever POW camps, cages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On several occasions you said "prisoners of war." What do you mean by this term? What does "prisoner of war" mean for you? What are the characteristics of a prisoner of war? How would you define this term?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: A prisoner of war should be a military person or a civilian who has -- who was taken while he was doing military activities which is not allowed. Somebody who is a civilian is not allowed to fight. But everybody who fights can be taken in prison as a POW. And he has to wear a uniform. And civilian people who are taken in prison are not POWs, for me. But I think that was a bit mixed up up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that means that the civilians who were present there could only have been arrested because they fought, they were under arms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: In my opinion. But I don't think that was always the case, of course. It should be, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another minor question, and then my colleague will ask you some further questions. Did your group have a liaison officer who was in contact with the BH army? Was there an officer at the site who acted as a liaison officer between your mission and the BH army? Did the BH army have -- had the BH army designated a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We hadn't a liaison officer in our group. Our group existed only of two monitors.
